newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban says foes killing its prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban says foes killing its prisoners.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement complained to the United Nations and the Red Cross on Sunday that the opposition northern alliance was killing Taleban prisoners, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said.

The complaint was made in letters given by the Taleban government's foreign ministry to U.N. and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) offices in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar, the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said, quoting Taleban sources.

It said the letters, signed by Foreign Minister Mullah Abdul Jalil, accused the opposition alliance of maltreating an unspecified number of Taleban fighters taken prisoner in late May in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif, capital of Balkh province serving as the headquarters of the alliance.
Groups of prisoners are daily taken out of prison and killed, it quoted the letters as saying.

It said the ministry's letters told the U.N. and ICRC offices that their staff, as well as journalists, could visit opposition fighters held by the Taleban, implying that similar visits should be allowed for Taleban prisoners.
AIP quoted a Taleban spokesman as saying 11 Taleban prisoners were killed in one incident when one fighter from the group escaped to tell the story of the alleged killings.

The opposition alliance says thousands of Taleban fighters and several officials were taken prisoner in late May when forces commanded by northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik drove the Taleban out of Mazar-i-Sharif only a few days after helping it to capture the town.

The officials reported to have been detained included then foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, who surfaced on July 24 in the northern province of Kunduz, saying he had avoided arrest and escaped with the help of some Mazar-i-Sharif citizens.
AIP said another Taleban figure, central committee member Mullah Mohammad Ibrahim, had also escaped from opposition-controlled territory and arrived in Kunduz three days ago.
The Taleban militia, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, including the capital Kabul, has set release of its prisoners as a precondition for peace talks with the alliance.
